title: Thread-Per-Request vs Event Loop
description: Compare the Apache thread-per-request model with Nginx's event-driven architecture, understand the C10K problem, and learn when each approach shines.

segments.text: Welcome back. Today we're diving into a fundamental architectural decision every web server makes: how do you handle thousands of connections at once? Two very different philosophies emerged.
The first approach is thread-per-request. Apache popularized this. A request arrives, a dedicated thread picks it up, handles the entire lifecycle, then returns to the pool. Simple and intuitive.

Each thread costs about one megabyte of stack memory. A thousand concurrent connections means a thousand threads, consuming a gigabyte of RAM just for stacks. And context switching between threads adds CPU overhead.
This is the C10K problem, named in 1999. How do you handle ten thousand concurrent connections on a single server? The thread-per-request model simply runs out of resources.
segments.thought_prompt: If threads are too expensive, how else could a server handle thousands of connections?

segments.text: Enter the event loop. Instead of one thread per connection, you have a single thread monitoring ALL connections. When data arrives on any socket, the event loop dispatches a callback. No blocking, no waiting.

Under the hood, event loops use OS primitives like epoll on Linux or kqueue on macOS. These let a single thread watch thousands of file descriptors simultaneously, getting notified only when something happens.

Nginx uses this model. With just a handful of worker processes, it can handle tens of thousands of concurrent connections using minimal memory. That's why it crushed Apache in benchmarks for static content.
But event loops have a catch. If any callback does heavy CPU work or blocks on a synchronous call, the entire loop stalls. Every connection freezes while that one task finishes.
segments.thought_prompt: When would you prefer threads over an event loop? Think about CPU-heavy workloads.

segments.text: Thread-per-request shines when each request does significant CPU work — image processing, complex calculations, machine learning inference. Threads let the OS schedule CPU time fairly across requests.

Event loops excel when requests are IO-bound — waiting on databases, calling external APIs, serving files. The server spends most of its time waiting, and event loops handle waiting extremely efficiently.

Modern servers often combine both. Nginx handles connections with an event loop, then proxies CPU-heavy work to threaded backends. Node.js uses an event loop but offloads blocking tasks to a thread pool.

The takeaway: there's no universal winner. Thread-per-request is simpler to reason about and great for CPU-bound work. Event loops dominate IO-bound scenarios. The best architectures use both strategically.
